description: We are a passionate team of AI enthusiasts and data analysts driven by a simple goal: turning complex  observation datasets into clear, impactful, and easy to use solutions. Whether we are spotting hidden environmental trends or building predictive models, we love bridging the gap between raw numbers and real-world problem solving.
summary:
"HeatShift: the summer moved. The work ban didn't."

HeatShift is an interactive web tool that checks whether heat-protection rules for outdoor workers still match the heat. Gulf countries protect millions of workers with fixed calendar bans; in Kuwait, no outdoor work from 11:00 to 16:00, 1 June to 31 August. Using 45 years of NASA POWER data for 20 cities, we found Kuwait's hot season has grown by about 13 days per decade (q = 0.006), confirmed by a NOAA weather station and ERA5. It now runs to about 11 September, and in all 7 Gulf ban cities it overruns the legal dates.

We converted NASA temperature and humidity into WBGT, the standard index of heat stress on workers. Every trend passes a prewhitened Mann-Kendall test, a red-noise check and a false-discovery-rate correction, and the key results are cross-checked against independent datasets.

Regulators can replay 45 summers, see the hours that fall outside each ban, and plan future ban dates while keeping today's working hours. HeatShift turns NASA Earth data into evidence for decisions that protect workers' health.
details:
What it does: HeatShift tests whether fixed midday work bans still protect outdoor workers. It uses NASA POWER daily data (1981–2025) and hourly data (2001–2025) for 20 cities. It computes each year's hot season and hourly heat stress (shade WBGT, with the wet bulb calculated from NASA temperature and humidity), and compares both with each country's legal ban.

How it works: every trend is tested (prewhitened Mann-Kendall, red-noise check, Theil-Sen slope with a 95% range, false-discovery-rate correction over 113 tests). Key results are cross-checked with a NOAA station and ERA5.

Benefits and impact: regulators, employers and NGOs can see that Kuwait's hot season now runs to about 11 September, past the 31 August end of the ban. They can replay 45 summers and plan ban dates for a future year while keeping today's working hours. The aim is evidence-based heat rules that protect workers' health.

Tools: Python (NumPy, pandas, SciPy), React, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, Chart.js, Vitest and Playwright. NASA POWER, NOAA GHCN-Daily and ISD, and ERA5 data. No paid APIs.

Creative: it turns a statistical trend into an interactive policy planner, with an evidence tooltip on every finding.

Factors considered: honest statistics and checks across datasets, international standards (ISO 7243), a phone-friendly design, and clear limits (not a forecast, not an injury count).
